catalog_quote: 9.1.3.4. Betonung a) Fast überall läßt sich die heutige Betonung auf die ältere quantitative Regel zurückführen, nach der die erste Gruppe v̄K oder vKK vom Wortende aus gesehen betont ist, spätestens jedoch der drittletzte Vokal. Dieses Prinzip ist trotz unterschiedlicher Entwicklung der Silbenstruktur meist noch erkennbar: Aar. ḍárabat, Mardin ḍárabət, Daragözü ẓárbət, Bagdad-Muslime ḍúrbat »sie schlug«; Aar. ḍarabátnī, Mardin ḍarabə́tni, Daragözü ẓərbə́tni, Bagdad-Muslime ḍurbátni »sie schlug mich« ... Bei der Behandlung geschlossener Silben, die sekundär durch Vokaleinschub oder -umsprung entstanden sind, gibt es zwei Möglichkeiten: Ein Teil der mesopotamischen Dialekte, und zwar sowohl qəltu- als gilit-Dialekte, hält an der ursprünglichen Betonung fest, obgleich sie der jetzigen Wortstruktur zuwiderläuft: (Mardin) ákəlna »unser Essen« ... ein anderer Teil paßt die Betonung der verän…

new_statements.quote: p. 92: "Demgegenüber ist der Wortakzent in den qD wie in vielen nar. Dialekten auf phonemischer Ebene beschränkt frei und somit beschränkt distinktiv." p. 94: "Betont ist, vom Wortende aus gesehen, das erste v̄ im Wortinlaut oder die erste Sequenz vKK, in Ermangelung dieser die erste Wortsilbe. Enklitika (durch einen Bindestrich an das vorhergehende Wort angeschlossen) zählen bei der Determination des Worttons nicht mit. Das gleiche gilt für den präfigierten bestimmten Artikel (3.1.5.) und präfigierte Präpositionen. Alle Abweichungen von dieser Grundregel werden durch Akut (') auf dem betonten Vokal gekennzeichnet."
new_statements.translation: p. 92: "By contrast, in the qəltu dialects, as in many Neo-Arabic dialects, the word accent is, at the phonemic level, free within limits and thus distinctive within limits." p. 94: "Stressed is, counted from the end of the word, the first (i.e. rightmost) word-internal long vowel or the first sequence vCC; failing these, the first syllable of the word. Enclitics (attached to the preceding word by a hyphen) do not count in determining the word accent. The same holds for the prefixed definite article (3.1.5.) and prefixed prepositions. All deviations from this basic rule are marked by an acute (') on the stressed vowel."
new_statements.citation: Jastrow, Otto. 1978. Die mesopotamisch-arabischen qəltu-Dialekte. Bd. I: Phonologie und Morphologie (Abhandlungen für die Kunde des Morgenlandes 43,4). Enklitik…
new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for nort3142 (catalog-all-2026-09-12) has an EMPTY rule and there are no existing statements, so this is the first sourced placement: Jastrow supplies a weight-sensitive default rule for the whole qəltu group plus a closed set of morphologically conditioned final-stress exceptions with dialect-by-dialect variation (Dēr izZōr, Kōsa, Mḥallami retract). Compatible with the empty record; adds the rule, the phonemic-within-limits status, the domain (enclitics, article, prepositions excluded) and the exceptions.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Default (quantity) rule for all qəltu dialects: stress the rightmost non-final heavy syllable (a syllable with a long vowel, or a vowel followed by two consonants); if there is none, stress the first syllable. Enclitics, the prefixed definite article and prefixed prepositions are outside the stress domain. Within the window between that heavy syllable and the word end the accent is 'restrictedly free' and phonemic: several morphological categories put stress on a later (final) syllable, so minimal pairs exist, e.g. Āzəx/Siirt qátalu 'they killed' : qatálu 'he killed him' : qatalú 'they killed him'; Mardin báyḍa 'egg' : bayḍá 'white (f.)' (p. 93). Jastrow argues (against Sasse) that the accent is phonemic precisely because it distinguishes morphological categories.
new_statements.exceptions: (a) p. 93 and p. 268: verbal object suffixes of series I and II always place stress on the syllable immediately preceding the suffix, i.e. the last syllable of the inflected verb, even when it is not heavy (Mardin qátal 'he killed' : qatálək 'he killed you (m)'; qəšáʕtən 'you (pl) saw' : qəšaʕtə́nu 'you (pl) saw him'); this holds in all qəltu dialects except Dēr izZōr, which follows the neighbouring gilit and Syrian sedentary dialects. (b) p. 31: final stress of nominal and verbal bases before pronominal relational (possessive) suffixes, e.g. Mardin baṣalə́tu 'his onion'; absent in Dēr izZōr (baṣalto). (c) pp. 31-32, 75-76: final stress in feminine forms of colour adjectives (Mardin sawdá, bayḍá; Āzəx bayẓá; Siirt bayvá; Christian/Jewish Baghdadi bedá/bidá), but the Kōsa and Mḥallami subdialects (Arbel, Kenderib báyḍa) and Dēr izZōr (sóda) have retracted the stress to the first syllable. (d) p. 92: in Kōsa, Mḥallami and Qarṭmīn the historical epenthetic vowel can bear stress (Qarṭmīn əḏə́nki), whereas in the other Anatolian dialects it cannot (Mardin ə́ḏənki, Siirt dárəbken).
new_statements.identity_note: Jastrow 1978 states the rule for the qəltu dialects as a group (Anatolian group: Mardin, Āzəx, Siirt, Daragözü, Kōsa, Mḥallami, Qarṭmīn, Diyarbakır; Tigris group: Mosul, Bəḥzāni, Christian and Jewish Baghdadi; Euphrates group: Dēr izZōr) and notes dialect-specific departures in the exceptions (Dēr izZōr has dropped the pre-object-suffix and pre-possessive final stress and, like Kōsa/Mḥallami, retracts colour-adjective stress to the first syllable). Lahdo 2009 describes Tillo, a Siirt-group qəltu dialect, and was not opened.

audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check passes: the deciding passage is verbatim on printed pp. 145-146 (PDF pp. 19-20) of the held archive.org scan of Jastrow 1980, page images read; the Ahmed 2018 corroborating locator (pp. 28-29) also matches the text we hold. (2) The classification rests on a 1980 handbook survey chapter by the leading authority on exactly this dialect group, so nothing suggests the classification (right-edge quantitative rule, v̄C/vCC heavy, three-syllable window, morphological final stress before pronominal suffixes, listed lexical exceptions) is wrong; but the chapter's stress paragraph is a diachronically framed condensation of Jastrow 1978 Bd. I, which we do not hold, and none of the six single-variety reference grammars in Glottolog's list is held either. Hence 'adequate' rather than 'well-sourced', and best_available_held = no. (3) The hedge in 'weight-hedged' is an artefact of the 1980 wording
